Threadfin porgy (Evynnis cardinalis) is a demersal sparid distributed along the continental shelf of the northwestern Pacific, where it supports important artisanal and commercial fisheries. Early life-history stages have been comparatively well described, with pelagic eggs hatching into yolk-sac larvae that undergo a rapid transition to exogenous feeding. At a water temperature of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], the incubation period lasts approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], after which the newly emerged prolarvae possess a modest yolk reserve that sustains them through the first days of non-feeding development. The wet weight at birth, estimated from the diameter of the fertilised ovum, is 0.00032 g [Wwb = 0.00032 g], a value consistent with the small pelagic eggs produced by other sparids of comparable size, such as Diplodus sargus. This low initial mass underscores the reliance on endogenous yolk nutrients prior to the onset of first feeding, which typically coincides with the completion of yolk-sac resorption and the development of a functional mouth gape.

As juveniles and sub-adults grow, the species exhibits a typical sparid growth trajectory with an asymptotic length parameter. Field surveys and length-frequency analyses indicate that the ultimate total length attained by adult Threadfin porgy reaches approximately 40 cm [Li = approximately 40 cm], a value comparable to that of other Evynnis species but modest relative to larger-bodied sparids like Dentex dentex. At the onset of puberty, individuals measure around 11.7 cm [Lp = around 11.7 cm] in total length, a threshold that corresponds to the initiation of gonadal recrudescence. The relationship between length and body mass, derived from empirical length-weight regressions, provides further insight into size at reproductive maturation. From the length at puberty, the predicted wet weight at puberty is 31.2 g [Wwp = 31.2 g], while the ultimate wet weight corresponding to the asymptotic length is 1248 g [Wwi = 1248 g]. These estimates place the species within the typical range of mass-at-length relationships documented for congeners in the region, where the condition factor generally approximates 0.01950.

Reproductive output in E. cardinalis has been characterised through histological analysis of gonadal tissue and field-based assessments of batch fecundity. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 5% [GSI = 5%] under the thermal conditions typical of the spawning period at 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C]. This relatively low value is consistent with a batch-spawning strategy in which the ovary does not accumulate a large mass of fully yolked oocytes at any single point, instead releasing smaller batches of hydrated eggs at intervals over the extended spawning season. Histological sections reveal asynchronous oocyte development, with the simultaneous presence of primary growth, cortical alveolar, and vitellogenic stages within the same ovary, indicating that females are capable of continuous or near-continuous egg production during the peak spawning months.

Longevity estimates for Threadfin porgy have been derived from otolith-based age validation studies and comparative data from related large-bodied sparids. The maximum recorded lifespan approaches 17 years [am = approaches 17 years] under stable environmental temperatures of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], a duration that aligns with the life-history pace of Dentex dentex, another moderately long-lived member of the Sparidae family. This extended longevity is characteristic of a species that matures relatively early — at a total length of 11.7 cm [Lp = 11.7 cm] — but continues somatic growth over many years, gradually approaching its asymptotic length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm]. The combination of early maturation, batch spawning, and a multi-decadal reproductive lifespan suggests an iteroparous strategy in which reproductive effort is distributed across numerous seasons, buffering the population against years of poor recruitment.

From a physiological perspective, the growth parameters of E. cardinalis reflect a pattern in which resources are directed toward both somatic development and reproductive output over its extensive lifespan. The wet weight at maturation, 31.2 g [Wwp = 31.2 g], represents less than three percent of the ultimate wet weight of 1248 g [Wwi = 1248 g], indicating that individuals invest heavily in post-maturation somatic growth. The small initial mass at hatching, 0.00032 g [Wwb = 0.00032 g], combined with a 5 day [ab = 5 day] incubation period at 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], typifies a high-fecundity, low-investment-per-offspring reproductive strategy common among demersal sparids. This life-history mosaic — rapid early development, modest size at puberty, substantial adult growth, and considerable longevity — allows E. cardinalis to persist under variable environmental conditions and moderate fishing pressure across its continental shelf habitat.
